title: Robert Kabera: Critic of Rwandan President Paul Kagame found beheaded in Uganda
description: A former Rwandan army sergeant major, who became an outspoken critic of President Paul Kagame, has been found beheaded in neighbouring Uganda.Robert K
body: A former Rwandan army sergeant major, who became an outspoken critic of President Paul Kagame, has been found beheaded in neighbouring Uganda.Robert Kabera, 50, fled Rwanda after being accused of sexual assault, which he denied. He sought asylum in neighbouring Uganda, citing political persecution.Ugandan police spokesperson Kituuma Rusoke on Monday said that Kabera's head had still not been recovered. His body was discovered by local residents on the outskirts of Kampala over the weekend. The Rwandan government has not publicly commented on the killing. Several critics of Kagame have been killed, both in Rwanda and abroad.His widow, Jeanne d'Arc Rwigema Uwizeye, told BBC Great Lakes in a written message that she now feared for her family's safety."It is scary. I feel crazy, the children and I don't have security," she said.According to his family, Kabera had travelled to inspect a construction site about 45 km (30 miles) outside Kampala before his death.Kabera built a public profile as a musician and YouTuber, attracting more than 144,000 subscribers to his channel, which featured over 800 videos, many criticising Kagame and his administration.Reacting to news of his murder, exiled opposition group Rwanda National Congress (RNC) called for a thorough investigation and for those responsible to be brought to justice.In a statement on X, the RNC said: "Today, his family is grieving, his voice is gone, and Rwandans in exile are confronting a terrifying question: where can we be safe?"His death adds to concerns about the safety of Rwandan dissidents living in exile.In 2014, Patrick Karegeya, a former Rwandan intelligence chief who helped set up the RNC, was found dead in his hotel room in Johannesburg, South Africa.Karegeya fell out with President Paul Kagame and was arrested twice, serving an 18-month prison sentence for insubordination and desertion before fleeing to South Africa in 2007, where he became a vocal critic of the government.Following his death, Kagame made remarks widely seen as a warning to other critics."Any person alive who may be plotting against Rwanda, whoever they are, will pay the price. Whoever it is, it is a matter of time," he said.In 2019, South African authorities issued arrest warrants for two Rwandans accused of murdering Karegeya.

schema.headline: Robert Kabera: Critic of Rwandan President Paul Kagame found beheaded in Uganda

title: Tiger Shroff: Bollywood actor survives shooting attempt in Mumbai
description: Police in India's Mumbai city are investigating a shooting attempt on Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff, who survived without sustaining any gunshot wounds
body: Police in India's Mumbai city are investigating a shooting attempt on Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff, who survived without sustaining any gunshot wounds.The 36-year-old was shot at on Sunday evening while he was in a car leaving a football ground in Juhu suburb. Videos showed at least two men firing multiple shots at close range at the front passenger seat of Shroff's car while it was moving slowly past a crowd.Two people, including Shroff's driver, were injured, according to the police. Three people were detained in Rajasthan on Monday in connection with the incident, the police said. The attack has sent shockwaves through Bollywood, with celebrities raising concerns about Shroff's safety. Several actors and political figures in Mumbai have been targeted by gunmen in recent years.Shroff, the son of veteran Bollywood actor Jackie Shroff, made his film debut with Heropanti in 2014. He has appeared in many action films, and is popular with fans for his dancing and martial arts skills.He is also a professional footballer and made his debut for Mumbay FC in October 2024 in a regional tournament. He was leaving the football ground after his regular practice session when the attack happenedEknath Shinde, deputy chief minister of Maharashtra state of which Mumbai is the capital, visited Shroff after the shooting on Sunday evening, and said the actor had been left "shaken" by the attack."These attempts to intimidate people will not be tolerated, and we will put an end to this hooliganism," Shinde said.In a photograph showing Shroff with Shinde, the actor is seen shirtless with some bandages on his upper body. It's not clear yet what injuries he sustained.Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis described the incident as "serious and condemnable", and said that the police would arrest some people "very soon".He said he had told Shroff that he should not worry, and that the government would ensure his "complete safety".Rajasthan police said two of the three suspects detained were from the northern states of Haryana and Bihar and had been living in Mumbai for the past few years. The third suspect is a minor.They are expected to be handed over to Mumbai Police later in the day.The All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA), a large union, condemned the attack, alleging that gangsters were deliberately targeting people in the film industry to create an "atmosphere of fear" and extort money from celebrities.In a statement, the association criticised the government and police for failing to prevent such attacks. It called for strict action against those responsible and better security for film industry workers and their families.The association also said the incident was a reminder of the 1990s, when criminal gangs wielded considerable influence in the city. It said that the film industry should not have to "work under the shadow of fear".Police have not yet confirmed who was behind the shooting. But Indian media reports have been widely reporting that an audio clip has surfaced in which a man claiming to be linked to the Lawrence Bishnoi gang says he is responsible.Bishnoi is currently lodged in a high-security prison in Gujarat state in connection with several high-profile cases.The authenticity of the recording and the man's claims have not been independently verified and police have not confirmed the gang's involvement yet.But the reports have brought the Bishnoi gang back into the headlines.In 2024, police arrested two people allegedly linked to the Bishnoi gang for a gun attack that targeted the home of Bollywood superstar Salman Khan.That same year, influential Indian politician Baba Siddique was shot dead in Mumbai. His murder, in a bustling neighbourhood in Mumbai, was also reportedly linked to people associated with the Bishnoi gang.Additional reporting by BBC Marathi

schema.headline: Tiger Shroff: Bollywood actor survives shooting attempt in Mumbai

title: Houthi missile strike on Yemen camp kills 50 security recruits, authorities say
description: More than 50 security personnel have been killed and 200 injured in a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's central province of Shabwa, local aut
body: More than 50 security personnel have been killed and 200 injured in a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's central province of Shabwa, local authorities say.A spokesman for the Saudi-backed Yemeni armed forces said the Iran-backed group launched three ballistic missiles at al-Alam camp near Ataq city, which was being used as a training centre for recruits to the security forces and police.The head of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, condemned what he called the "criminal attack" and promised a "firm response".The Houthis' military spokesman said they had targeted "Saudi enemy concentrations".Yemen's devastating civil war has flared up in recent months.At the start of October, pro-government forces launched a major offensive that aims to retake territory in western Yemen that is controlled by the Houthis.With air support from a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states, they managed to regain control of territory on the Red Sea coast that overlooks the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, which the Houthis captured in a surprise assault in September.However, fierce fighting is continuing there, as well as around the besieged government-controlled city of Taiz, and to the north in Marib and al-Jawf provinces.The Houthis have also responded to the Saudi air strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases in neighbouring Saudi Arabia.Monday's attack in Shabwa is one of the deadliest reported since the start of the escalation.Shabwa province's media office said in a statement that ballistic missiles struck the Martyr Ahmed al-Sulaimani Training Centre, where recruits from several provinces were undergoing training to be members of the internal security forces. According to a preliminary assessment, 53 were killed and more than 200 injured, it added.A video posted on social media appeared to show several bodies scattered across the ground.Shabwa's deputy governor, Fahad al-Khalifi, told AFP news agency that hospitals in the province were overwhelmed and had been forced to transfer the most seriously wounded to neighbouring Hadramout and Aden, where the government is based. Some of them were in a critical condition, he said.Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said the attack constituted a war crime because the internal security forces training centre was not a military target.He also accused the Houthis of "attempting to fabricate a false media victory, boost the morale of its collapsing elements, and cover up the defeats and setbacks it is suffering across various combat axes".The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said in a statement that the missiles targeted a gathering of "Saudi enemy" forces at al-Alam camp, which he said was run by Saudi officers.There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities.In a separate development, Houthi-run media reported that a Saudi air strike on a home in the Sahar district of the Houthi-controlled northern province of Saada on Sunday killed at least 10 people and injured 23 others, many of them women and children.According to the Houthi-run health ministry in north-western Yemen, a total of 141 people had been killed in Saudi strikes over the past seven weeks.The government's health ministry, meanwhile, said last week that at least 1,282 people had been killed in the conflict across Yemen since 6 August.In Saudi Arabia, at least 19 people have been killed in Houthi attacks targeting the kingdom's airports since the beginning of October.Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

schema.headline: Houthi missile strike on Yemen camp kills 50 security recruits, authorities say

title: Protesters and police in Albania fight in seventh day of violent clashes
description: Protesters in Albania have fought with riot police on the seventh consecutive day of violent clashes.The protesters, many of them high school and univ
body: Protesters in Albania have fought with riot police on the seventh consecutive day of violent clashes.The protesters, many of them high school and university students, are trying to oust embattled Prime Minister Edi Rama. Official figures said 295 people have been injured, 186 of whom are police officers, before Monday's violence."The moment the state negotiates with this," Rama told grim-faced police chiefs, brandishing a rock hurled at police on Sunday, "the state has fallen".A police station and government buildings in Tirana have been attacked during the protests, which are being driven by demands for better university conditions, anger over corruption and calls for Rama's resignation.The protesters included "young men and women who have been radicalised by dark forces in Europe and the US", Rama said. "Albania has become one of the targets of a well co-ordinated attack."In brilliant October sunshine in Rinia Park, also known as Youth Park, I watched people prising loose cobble stones - like that brandished by the prime minister - as ammunition for later battles with police. They did not have long to wait.A convoy of police vehicles advanced down a broad boulevard, led by an armoured truck firing water cannon and tear gas canisters among the fleeing protesters.Squads of riot police chased the predominantly student crowd through the park. Protesters took refuge in a cafe where even the eyes of the waiters streamed from the teargas.Under trees, volunteers in yellow reflector jackets stood their ground helping those overcome by the fumes. I watched a young man remonstrating with a policeman, who then fired pepper spray in his face at point-blank range."The police actions are often chaotic and stupid," human rights lawyer Gentian Sejrani told the BBC. He provides legal support to more than 100 people who have been arrested."In court, the police rarely present evidence," he said. His clients include a man arrested on his way to a bus stop – completely unrelated to the protests, he said."Those who are actually throwing stuff at the police rarely get caught, because they run the fastest," Serjani said.Police appear as incensed by the violence against their colleagues as the protesters are by the strong-arm tactics of the police. The result is mayhem.Outside the cafe in the park, when the gas has cleared, 27-year-old activist Sidorela Vatnikaj, a masters student, describes her typical day. In a movement without leaders she is one of the more experienced, with eight years in the forefront of anti-government protests behind her."In the morning, you try to co-ordinate with all the groups - where they are, and where the protest is taking place. If any lawyers are needed, if any first aid kit or any kind of equipment is needed. And you also have to make sure all your friends, your family members in the protest are OK."The day is spent going from protest to protest, much of it running from police, she said.She is uncomfortable with the violence towards the authorities from her fellow protesters, but blames the police for starting and fuelling it."When I see people throwing stones at the police, I understand their anger. I don't judge them. I'm not happy, but they have no other way to be listened to," Vatnikaj said."They come from families whose family members had no other choice than to leave the country - a million in the past decade. They have not only been robbed, they have been bullied, ignored and now they they have also been beaten up."At the weekend, the prime minister asked rhetorically what would happen if he stepped down."We need a technocratic government for one year, to prepare the country for real, democratic elections," Vatnikaj replies. She has accused Rama of rigging previous elections, and of being hand in glove with rich foreign investors and organised crime groups.Young people in Albania feel encouraged by their fellow Gen Z protesters around the world, Vatnikaj said."I have seen my mother and father's generation, working all their lives and dreaming of having a democratic society where they could live with dignity. That never happened," she said.Rama has been in power for 13 years, and has been a dominant figure in Albanian politics since the turn of the century. He has promised EU membership by 2030, and said he is the only one who can deliver it.

schema.headline: Protesters and police in Albania fight in seventh day of violent clashes

title: Lula and Bolsonaro trade barbs in Brazil election debate
description: Brazil's left-wing President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his right-wing rival, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, have clashed in a debate held one week be
body: Brazil's left-wing President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his right-wing rival, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, have clashed in a debate held one week before the run-off presidential election.Polls suggest the two candidates are neck and neck and the televised debate was  hailed as a chance for both to sway undecided voters. But the showdown was marked by personal attacks and analysts have warned that its aggressive tone may increase the abstention rate further.In the first round of voting, held on 4 October, Bolsonaro defied opinion polls by securing a narrow lead over Lula. Sunday's debate was the first of two before the vote. The second is planned for Friday, just two days before polls open.Flávio Bolsonaro is standing for the Liberal Party after his father, Jair Bolsonaro - who governed from 2018 to 2022 - was sentenced to more than 20 years in prison for plotting to overthrow Lula after the latter beat him in the 2022 election. The younger Bolsonaro won 47% of the vote in the first round, compared with Lula's 45.2%, with both falling short of the 50% of the valid votes needed to stave off a decisive second round. Since the return to democracy in 1988, there has been no instance in which the candidate who lost in the first round went on to win in the second but Lula has told his supporters that he will "win in extra time". Analysts consulted by BBC News Brasil were struck by how much the debate was dominated not by issues but personal attacks.Yuri Sanches from pollsters AtlasIntel said it was a debate in which no policies were discussed and there were no rational arguments. "The independent voter, who is sometimes against Bolsonaro and sometimes against the Workers' Party [of Lula], came out of it with a very negative impression."Lucas Aragão from political analysis firm Arko Advice said Bolsonaro had appeared calmer during the debate and seemed to have managed to "get under Lula's skin". Rafael Cortez from consulting firm da Tendências Consultoria, however, argued that Lula had managed to score a goal when he said he would open up his financial and phone records and those of his family to judicial scrutiny, and challenged his rival to do the same before Sunday's run-off.Many observers criticised the format of the debate, which was described as chaotic at times, with each of the candidates pacing around the TV studio as the other was speaking.One heated exchange saw Bolsonaro telling Lula he should come stand next to him so that the two could talk.Referring to alleged links between the senator and paramilitary vigilante groups, Lula said "I don't want to be close to you", and that he wanted to maintain "distance from the Bolsonaro family" and "the militia". Bolsonaro, who has dismissed the allegations as fake news, in turn tried to bait Lula by saying, "On second thoughts, maybe it's better to keep my distance so that my wallet isn't stolen."He also accused the Workers' Party of being corrupt, holding up the palm of his hand on which he had scribbled "CORRUPTO" (Portuguese for "corrupt)."Take a piece of paper and a pen and jot down 'corrupt' and you'll see that it has two letters in the middle here together," he said, pointing to PT, the initials of the Workers' Party in Portuguese. Bolsonaro, who is campaigning on a iron-fist approach to crime, challenged Lula to explain why crime rates had gone up during his four years in power. He also alleged, without providing any evidence, that "the majority of convicts vote for Lula".Lula shot back with a thinly veiled reference to Flávio's convicted father, Jair, saying; "I wish it was 100%, even your father".

schema.headline: Lula and Bolsonaro trade barbs in Brazil election debate

title: Japan's MMX mission set to grab a piece of Mars's moon Phobos
description: Mission blasts off for Mars to grab a piece of its moonFigure caption, Watch: Spacecraft heading to Mars' moon Phobos lifts off from JapanByRebecca Mo
body: Mission blasts off for Mars to grab a piece of its moonFigure caption, Watch: Spacecraft heading to Mars' moon Phobos lifts off from JapanByRebecca MorelleAlison Francis and Kevin ChurchBBC News Science  A spacecraft has launched from Japan headed for Mars' moon Phobos, where it will attempt to grab some moondust and bring it back to Earth.If it is successful, this will become the first time a sample has been returned from Mars or its moons to be analysed in laboratories here on Earth. The spacecraft is scheduled to arrive at Phobos in August 2027.It is hoped that the Mars Moons Exploration (MMX) mission, which is led by the Japanese Space Agency, will solve the mystery of how Mars's moons formed.Prof Sara Russell, from the Natural History Museum, who is the MMX mission's deputy for sample analysis, said: "There hasn't yet been a successful mission to go to Phobos and bring a bit back to Earth. "I think this is an incredibly ambitious and fun mission," she said.There are only three moons in the inner Solar System: our own Moon, and two around Mars, which are called Phobos and Deimos.Both of these are tiny - Phobos is about 20km (12 miles) across and Deimos is about 10km (six miles) across. They are also irregularly shaped, looking a bit like space potatoes.The MMX spacecraft will study Deimos as it arrives in the Mars neighbourhood, and then will focus on Phobos.It plans to set down a small rover to explore the terrain, though this will be no easy feat.Sara Russell says no one has ever landed a rover on such a small moon."The moon itself doesn't have very much of its own gravity," she explained."But it's next to an enormous planet that's got a much higher gravity,  and that makes it much harder to get a rover onto the surface."Image source, NASAImage caption, Mars got its moons about 4.5bn years ago - but no one knows how they formedThe rover will scout out a landing site so that the MMX spacecraft itself can later touch down on Phobos.Once on the surface, it will deploy a robotic arm and two samplers to grab some moon dust.This material will be packed into a small capsule that will return to Earth in 2031, landing in the Woomera desert of South Australia.The amount of material that will come back is tiny - just 10g."It's a very small [amount] actually," said Dr Chrysa Avdellidou, from Leicester University, who is working with the Japanese mission.   "However we can do several studies even on individual grains… You don't need to have kilos back from a surface in order to do science.  So it's worth every gram," she said.Image source, JAXAImage caption, The spacecraft will collect 10g of moon dust from the surface of PhobosScientists believe the sample will finally shed light on the puzzle of where Mars's moons came from.There are two competing ideas.Either a space rock smashed into Mars early in its history, and Phobos and Deimos were created from the debris.Or the moons are two wandering asteroids from the outer Solar System, which were grabbed by the Red Planet's gravity."When we get the sample back, we'll be able to look in detail at its chemistry and its mineral composition - and the two hypotheses will produce very distinct results," said Sara Russell."It should be pretty much immediately obvious.. whether it's the product of this dramatic impact or whether it's a captured asteroid. So we'll find that out really quickly."The team is also hoping there might be an extra bonus coming back to their labs."One of the really exciting things is that Phobos is so close to the Mars surface that whenever there's an impact into the Mars surface, little grains might actually become implanted into Phobos itself," said Russell."And that means that the sample we get back may actually contain grains of Mars as well. So it can give us really direct information about the composition and history of Mars."Image source, Kevin Church/BBC NewsImage caption, Martian meteorites are rare - this one is on display at the Natural History Museum  Bringing material from Mars back to Earth has long been an ambition of space scientists.The Nasa Perseverance rover, which has been exploring Mars since 2021, has been carefully collecting samples on Mars and storing them in canisters.But a second Nasa/ESA mission, called Mars Sample Return, that would have picked up and returned these canisters, has been effectively cancelled, after its funding was halted by the US Congress.China is planning its own sampling mission to Mars, set to launch in 2028. It will attempt to return Martian material to Earth in 2031.We do already have some fragments of the Red Planet here on Earth in the form of Martian meteorites.These are pieces of Mars that were blasted off the surface by asteroid strikes, and ended up being hurled towards the Earth.Martian meteorites are extremely rare, but like all space rocks that fall to our planet, they become contaminated as soon as they get here, mixing with the air, dust, soil and water.Scientists are so desperate to get their gloved hands on a direct sample from Mars and its moons because it would be pristine.

schema.headline: Japan's MMX mission set to grab a piece of Mars's moon Phobos

title: Italy plans tougher security measures after violent Milan protests
description: Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is poised to approve emergency security measures, according to local media, after protests over rising costs bro
body: Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is poised to approve emergency security measures, according to local media, after protests over rising costs broke out into violent clashes in Milan.The measures include extending preventative detention to minors and restricting group gatherings, Milanese paper Corriere della Sera reported.Police deployed tear gas and water cannons after protesters - many in masks - threw paving stones, bins and chairs at officers over the weekend. More than 250 people were detained, 80% of whom were minors, Italian police said.The expected crackdown comes after Meloni chaired an emergency security meeting on Monday afternoon. No official announcements have been made.More than 5,000 people gathered in Milan over the weekend. As well as clashes between police and some protesters, stores were looted and property was set on fire.High-end shops in the city's centre closed early on Monday, with many boarding up their windows over fears of further damage. Measures to crack down on youth gangs are expected to be approved as early as Tuesday as part of a decree law, according to Corriere della Sera.Local media reports suggest social media was used to invite young people to Italy's squares over the weekend.Rioting and violence have broken out on the sidelines of mostly peaceful youth-led protests in other European countries including France, Spain and Albania, in recent weeks.Milanese Mayor Giuseppe Sala said he was worried this represented a "new phenomenon" that "originates from an international scenario and therefore feeds itself".Speaking to Ansa, he said he witnessed "smashed shop windows, looted stores, and frightened citizens", adding that "what happened here is what we are seeing in many cities around the world".Of the 271 people taken to police stations on Sunday, 32 were arrested, including 23 minors, police said on Monday. A further 28 people were reported to judicial authorities.Italian media reported that people - including police officers - were injured. Violence between protesters and police also spread to other cities in the north.Meloni said people in Turin were detained while "carrying cobblestones and window-breaking hammers", while a train station in Bologna was closed as a precaution after similar disorder."To demonstrate is a right. To lay our cities to waste is not," Meloni said on Saturday, adding that "hooligans" had exploited the protests to "sow chaos".The prime minister - who is facing an election next year - also called on her political opponents to condemn the rioting."Do not be ambiguous about this," she said in a post on X, explaining that condemnation must be "unanimous" because "any hesitation becomes justification".Democratic Party leader Elly Schlein said her party had always condemned violence and that the rioting should not be used to stifle the voices of peaceful protesters across the country who are struggling to make a living, Ansa reported.The violent disorder followed anti-government protests held by students in various Italian cities on Friday, and echoed similar unrest in neighbouring France, where hundreds of thousands took to the streets.

schema.headline: Italy plans tougher security measures after violent Milan protests

title: Tennis star Svitolina says emotional toll of Ukraine war led to Monfils separation
description: Ukrainian tennis star Elina Svitolina has announced the end of her marriage with French former tennis player Gaël Monfils, citing the emotional impact
body: Ukrainian tennis star Elina Svitolina has announced the end of her marriage with French former tennis player Gaël Monfils, citing the emotional impact of the war in her country.The 32-year-old, who is ranked number six in the world, wrote in a heartfelt post on Instagram about the effect the conflict and "what the war has done to me inside". "This is the most difficult thing I have ever had to share," she wrote, saying "I need to find my way back to myself". Svitolina said she felt she could not do that within her marriage.She said her husband Monfils, 40, "listened" and "respected what I need with a strength and grace I will never forget". "Some battles happen deep inside you, and no amount of love from someone else can win them for you," the four-time Grand Slam semi-finalist wrote.It was "the hardest thing I have ever had to tell the person I love", Svitolina said."Everyone knows how much Ukraine means to me," Svitolina, who grew up in Odesa, said. Ukraine's Black Sea port city has been heavily bombed by Russia throughout the war.Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022."What you didn't see were the sleepless nights, the doubts, and the feeling of slowly losing myself."The tennis power couple married in 2021 and have one child together - a four-year-old daughter called Skai.Svitolina said her daughter "will always come first", adding "our marriage is ending, but our family is not".Monfils, a former world number six, was expected to play the final tournament of his career at next month's Paris Masters in an emotional farewell.However, the two-time Grand Slam semi-finalist's retirement was effectively confirmed last week when he appeared on the International Tennis Integrity Authority's list of retired players.Once a player removes themselves from anti-doping protocols, they are not eligible to compete in professional tournaments.Monfils, who won 13 titles on the ATP Tour, is preparing to start a new career in finance after joining a Swiss wealth management firm.

schema.headline: Tennis star Svitolina says emotional toll of Ukraine war led to Monfils separation

title: Deadly fire at Canada military base moved a kilometre 'in 30 to 60 seconds'
description: A fire that killed four members of the Canadian military and injured dozens of others on Saturday spread with alarming speed, accounts suggest.It brok
body: A fire that killed four members of the Canadian military and injured dozens of others on Saturday spread with alarming speed, accounts suggest.It broke out in a grassy training area at a base in the province of Alberta and spread rapidly due to strong winds."The fire was 1km (0.6 miles) away when the wind shifted," said Maj-Gen Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division of the Canadian Armed Forces. "It is not normal for a fire to move a kilometre in 30 to 60 seconds."Prime Minister Mark Carney described it as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime". Officials have ruled out the possibility of "any terrorist activity".Speaking in the House of Commons on Monday, Carney said the fire was "driven by ferocious winds". "The fire jumped nearly a kilometre less than a minute to where the soldiers were gathered," he said, adding that the cause of the fire was not yet known.Carney said the injuries occurred "in the space of a few minutes".The blaze began at about 16:00 (22:00 GMT) on Saturday at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, one of the country's busiest military training bases. Carney confirmed that Sgt Morgan Wong, Pte Shaun Farrell, Pte Aidan Goulding and Pte Hayden Lykkemark have died.He said the troops were preparing to be sent to Latvia and were training to join the Canadian Armed Forces' Global Response Task Force, "which can deploy within hours anywhere in the world Canada needs them".Of the 39 injured people receiving care in hospital, at least 19 are in a critical condition. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department doctor at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told Canadian broadcaster CBC that the number of patients involved in the incident had "completely overwhelmed" healthcare facilities in Wainwright.Tributes are being paid to the servicemen who died. Patricia Farrell, the mother of Shaun Farrell, wrote on Facebook that it was "with heavy hearts that we share the news that our son, Shaun Farrell, has passed away to be with our Heavenly Father".Wong received a tribute from the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, of which he was part. The regiment was "deeply saddened", it wrote in a Facebook post of its own. It sent "heartfelt condolences to [the group's] families, friends, and fellow soldiers".The mother of Goulding, Sonia Monk, said her late son was an exceptional athlete and a natural leader. "He was always the guy who kept everybody's spirits up," she told CBC. "He really was the light of my life."Canadian PM Carney said on Monday that Goulding was known as "a generous and deeply loyal friend". Lykkemark, Carney said, "was known for his gift for lightening a hard day, his quick wit - he dreamed of a career in law enforcement". "These were sons, brothers, partners, friends, young men with bright futures who chose to serve our country and who died in that cause," Carney said. Forecasters had issued a wind warning on Saturday for large parts of Alberta, predicting wind gusts of up to 90km/h (66mph), Canadian broadcaster CBC said.According to Rutland, the investigation may take at least a month.Wainwright, about 130 miles east of Edmonton, Alberta's capital, is one of the main bases used by the Canadian military for live-fire training exercises, and it houses troops from Canada and allied countries. About 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers are on site on a typical day.The fire erupted just before Albertans voted to decide whether the province should separate from Canada. Defence minister David McGuinty declined to comment on Saturday when asked whether it would impact the election. "This is not the time to speak about that issue at this stage," he said.

schema.headline: Deadly fire at Canada military base moved a kilometre 'in 30 to 60 seconds'

title: Suspect arrested after Limoges town hall set alight during disorder - French media
description: Figure caption, ByJacob PhillipsUpdated 2 minutes agoA suspect linked to a far-left movement has been arrested in France after a 19th Century city hal
body: Figure caption, ByJacob PhillipsUpdated 2 minutes agoA suspect linked to a far-left movement has been arrested in France after a 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire over the weekend that broke out during mass disorder, French media report.The clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall in the central city of Limoges were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday.The 40-year-old suspect is known for acts of violence against public officials and has been classified as an "S" subject, meaning he is a potential threat to national security, FranceInfo reported.More than 120 people have already been imprisoned following widespread demonstrations across France, French Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin told CNews-Europe.Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets to protest against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.Darmanin said he asked prosecutors to be "extremely firm" and "ruthless towards those who attacked police officers, gendarmes and firefighters, who looted shops and who attacked public buildings".The justice minister insisted France did not need to be put into a state of emergency which would "deprive all French people of their individual freedoms".But French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu earlier said he had not ruled out imposing a state of emergency.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, The city hall's roof and clock tower in Limoges was severely damaged in the fireTargeted curfews introduced across France on Monday contributed to a quiet night following the disorder, Lecornu said.Curfews were introduced across parts of central Paris, including Place de la République, where protesters had gathered over the weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area.Other measures restricting the movement of young people and gatherings were introduced in cities such as Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south, as well as Lille and other towns in the north.Lecornu thanked police officers and gendarmes for enforcing the measures, adding that further curfews on Tuesday night would be decided depending on where they were necessary.Writing in a post on X, he said decisions would be made "on the ground" by French regions and local mayors.Image source, Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, The streets in the southern city of Lyon were quiet on Monday nightEarlier Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez admitted police had "lost control" in some cities.He was strongly criticised by opposition politicians over authorities' preparedness for the disorder, leading him to offer his resignation on Monday, which was rejected by President Emmanuel Macron.More than 2,500 people have been arrested since the disorder broke out, officials said on Monday. One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency. About 1,000 police officers were injured.Protests first began last month with students demanding better school conditions but they have escalated to take in a broader range of concerns with numbers at demonstrations bolstered by trade unions and various protest groups.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Riots took place across French cities, including the capital ParisMore than 2,000 shops and other businesses have been directly impacted by the weekend's violence, the head of France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) said.Rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings and looting businesses in Paris, Marseille and other cities and smaller towns.Protest organisers have declared that a second round of protests will take place on Saturday across France.The so-called yellow vests (gilets jaunes), who were responsible for France's longest-ever modern protests in 2018, has said "Act II" will take place this weekend.

schema.headline: Suspect arrested after Limoges town hall set alight during disorder - French media

title: In pictures: Dussehra celebrated across India as a symbol of good over evil
description: Image source, APImage caption, The festival includes a variety of celebrations involving actors playing deities - pictured here an actor portraying Lo
body: Image source, APImage caption, The festival includes a variety of celebrations involving actors playing deities - pictured here an actor portraying Lord Ram prepares ahead of a procession in Prayagraj, Uttar PradeshByRachita PrasadBBC News, MumbaiMillions of people across India are marking Dussehra, one of the country's most widely celebrated Hindu festivals, with processions, prayers and the ceremonial burning of giant effigies to symbolise the triumph of good over evil.The festival is observed with different rituals and traditions across different parts of the country but with grand celebrations everywhere.It commonly marks the deity Lord Ram's victory over the mythological 10-headed king Ravan. The festival coincides with Vijayadashami, celebrated in eastern, southern and other parts of India, to honour goddess Durga slaying the buffalo demon Mahishasura.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Giant effigies of the 10-headed king Ravan are brought out and burnt as part of festivities in AhmedabadImage source, Hindustan Times via Getty ImagesImage caption, Ramlila, a theatrical performance based on the Hindu epic Ramayan, is performed as part of Dussehra celebrations, seen here in NoidaImage source, Hindustan Times via Getty ImagesImage caption, The vanquishing of the 10-headed king Ravan is celebrated as the victory of righteousness over evil, with Sita placing a victory garland around the neck of her husband Lord RamImage source, Hindustan Times via Getty ImagesImage caption, Smaller Ravan effigies are a common sight at markets ahead of the Dussehra festivities, such as at this one in Delhi Image source, EPAImage caption, The festival is celebrated in different ways across the country - here, people buy flowers at a market in Bengaluru ahead of DussehraImage source, NurPhoto via Getty ImagesImage caption, Marigolds are associated with the celebrations as a symbol of the victory of good over evil, harvested ahead of Dussehra around the countryHindus follow a lunar calendar, and Dussehra falls on the 10th day after Navratri, a nine-night festival of worship and celebrations.In the days leading up to Dussehra in northern India, performers wear elaborate costumes and make-up to stage Ramlila, the dramatic retelling of the ancient Hindu epic Ramayana. They recount Lord Ram's exile and his wife Sita's abduction by Ravan, culminating in the battle that symbolises the victory of good over evil. The final act is followed by the ritualistic burning of the effigies of Ravan, his brother, Kumbhkaran, and son Meghnath.The vibrant stage is usually accompanied by a carnival-like atmosphere with food stalls, rides and smaller performances.Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty ImagesImage caption, Ramlila performances often coincide with wider family-friendly events including stalls and rides, as pictured here in NoidaIn the east and some other parts, as well as among Hindus in Bangladesh, the festival sees devotees worshipping the divine feminine power with Durga Puja celebrations.Temporary tents housing idols of Goddess Durga and other deities are set up across cities and towns. People visit these structures, known as pandals, where Durga is often depicted slaying the buffalo demon Mahishasura.Current affairs often make their way into the traditional celebrations, like theme-based decoration of tents in Kolkata city, which is famous for its Durga Puja celebrations. Image source, NurPhoto via Getty ImagesImage caption, Goddess Durga is depicted in celebrations as part of Durga Puja, who is said to have slayed the buffalo demon Mahishasura - artisans work on idols for weeks ahead of the event, as seen here in KolkataImage source, APImage caption, Devotees light oils lamps during Sandhi Puja, an auspicious moment of Durga PujaImage source, NurPhoto via Getty ImagesImage caption, Elaborate and artistic temporary tents are set up to house idols for Durga PujaImage source, NurPhoto via Getty ImagesImage caption, Traditional dances such as Gujarat's Garba form a key part of community celebrationsDussehra also marks the beginning of preparations for Diwali - the festival of lights - which is held 20 days later.

schema.headline: In pictures: Dussehra celebrated across India as a symbol of good over evil

title: How is the US economy really doing under President Trump?
description: ByBen ChuPolicy and analysis correspondentPresident Donald Trump has been boasting about the performance of the US economy ahead of the midterm congre
body: ByBen ChuPolicy and analysis correspondentPresident Donald Trump has been boasting about the performance of the US economy ahead of the midterm congressional elections, claiming he has boosted incomes, reduced inflation and created jobs.Trump has repeatedly said: "We have the hottest country anywhere in the world."While the overall US economy is faring better than many expected after Trump launched his sweeping "Liberation Day" tariffs in 2025, there's evidence those import taxes and the impact of the US-Israel war with Iran have pushed up inflation, with the harmful effects felt by most American households.The US economy is also being helped by an AI investment boom, and could falter if that spending were to dry up.So how does all this feel for the average American? BBC Verify has looked at whether the evidence supports the president's claims. 1. US economy growingThe overall US economy is growing at a respectable clip by the country's recent historic standards.The latest data shows US GDP, external - which is how economists measure the size of the US economy - currently expanding at an annualised rate of 2.2%.And it has increased by around 3.2% overall since the end of 2024, just before Trump took office for his second term.That is more growth than any other member of the G7 group of leading economies over that period.The US growth rate has been faster than was forecast by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), external in the immediate wake of Trump's announcement of a swathe of new tariffs on goods coming into the US on 2 April 2025.It downgraded its forecasts at the time, citing the negative impact of Trump's import duties on investment and consumer spending.Though it is important to note that Trump eased the tariffs considerably in the months that followed, reducing the impact that had initially been expected on the economy.The US economy has also been heavily supported in recent years by American technology companies making massive investments in AI, including by constructing data centres around the country.Spending on building data centres, external (excluding the IT hardware to go in them) by US businesses in August 2026 was $5bn, almost double the monthly rate when Trump returned to office. 2. Inflation picked upMany American voters wanted to punish Joe Biden in the 2024 presidential election, holding him responsible for the pain caused by a significant spike in prices in the wake of the pandemic.The current rate of US inflation, external is 3.7%. That's still well down on the recent peak rate of 9% under Biden in 2022, but higher than the 3% rate that Donald Trump inherited in January 2025.Economists estimate, external US inflation would have been lower without the new tariffs imposed by Trump since he returned to office.While the impact of the Iran war on global energy prices, with the significant disruption to oil and fuel supplies from the Middle East, has also helped push up US domestic inflation.3. Household income growth held backAverage US household incomes are still rising under Trump.The median income - after adjusting for inflation - rose 2.6% in 2025 to $87,460, the highest on record, external.However, the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy (ITEP) think tank has estimated the combined effects of the following, external on US households:- Trump's tax cuts- The expiry of extra government subsidies that had made health insurance cheaper for millions of Americans- Higher-than-expected price rises during Trump's second term, including those linked to tariffs and the Iran warITEP's conclusion is that the middle fifth of households are, on average, around $1,700 worse off in 2026 than they would have been, while the poorest fifth are around $750 worse off.The richest 1%, by contrast, are estimated to be an average of $12,560 better off than they woud have been, primarily because of Trump's tax cuts.ITEP's estimates about the impact of tariffs on American households of different income levels are broadly similar to those of the Tax Foundation think tank, external.4. Job creation slowed downTrump predicted his tariffs would result in America being "flooded with jobs", external as manufacturing firms set up new factories on US soil to avoid their products being taxed at the border.Since he returned to the White House, an average of 34,000 jobs have been added to the economy each month.​​But that is significantly down on the 122,000 jobs added each month in the final year of Biden's presidency, external.5. Borrowing costs risingThe growing deficit is also one of the reasons the US government gets charged more to borrow money in financial markets.The 10-year US government bond yield has risen sharply since Trump returned to office in January 2025 and is now above 5%, the highest rate since the global financial crisis in 2007.That increase in the market cost of US government borrowing also puts upward pressure on the interest rates on mortgages available to American households.The interest rate on a new 30-year US mortgage has risen to 7.4%, external per year, up from 6.9% when Trump returned to the White House.That's added to problems in the US housing market, making homes less affordable for new buyers. It has left many existing owners reluctant to move because doing so would mean giving up their cheaper mortgages, which they took out at lower rates, external and cannot take with them to a new property.Data graphics by Erwan Rivault.

schema.headline: How is the US economy really doing under President Trump?

title: Fatima El Mansouri: What can Morocco's first female prime minister change for women?
description: The Islamic saying "a people who entrust their affairs to a woman will never succeed" has resurfaced in Morocco since King Mohammed VI named Fatima Za
body: The Islamic saying "a people who entrust their affairs to a woman will never succeed" has resurfaced in Morocco since King Mohammed VI named Fatima Zahra El Mansouri as the country's first female prime minister.Mustafa Ramid, a former justice minister in an Islamist-led government, cited the saying earlier this month, in a lengthy Facebook post questioning whether a woman should hold the country's highest political office.He argued that Morocco, a Muslim majority country, had found a balance between equality and the responsibilities of state leadership, as the highest office - that of the king - continued to be reserved for men.Morocco operates as a constitutional monarchy. Yet executive power remains in the hands of the 63-year-old monarch. El Mansouri's Authenticity and Modernity Party (Pam) won the most seats in September's parliamentary election and has since announced a coalition with three other parties. Together, they hold 207 of the 395 seats in parliament.El Mansouri's royal appointment was historic but it exposed persistent reservations about women in positions of power.The day after her appointment, local broadcaster Chouf TV took to the streets to ask Moroccan men "what they thought" of a woman heading the government.Several men, mostly middle-aged or older, hesitated before answering. Some said they accepted the decision because it was the king's choice.One grey-haired man, who did not give his name or age, said: "It feels strange to have a woman as head of government. I'm not sure if it sits well with me."Criticism of the monarchy carries legal risks in Morocco. The penal code criminalises certain forms of offence or insult against the king, the royal family and the monarchy.Online, the appointment became fodder for political satire. A video showing two women pulling each other's hair was widely shared, with captions suggesting that this is what parliamentary disagreements between El Mansouri and her colleagues might look like.However many younger Moroccans, especially women, welcomed her appointment.While attitudes are changing in Morocco, conservative, religious views still hold great weight.Some of the country's most contentious debates over gender equality centre on family law, including inheritance, marriage and divorce.Under existing inheritance rules, a daughter typically receives half the share of a son in comparable circumstances. The Higher Council of Ulemas, the country's body of religious scholars, has resisted calls for equal inheritance, citing Islamic jurisprudence.It has also rejected proposals to abolish taasib, a rule that can require female orphans without brothers to share their inheritance with male relatives, including distant ones. In a 2022 report, Morocco's National Human Rights Council said unequal inheritance rules contributed to poverty among women.Polygamy is also legal under certain conditions. Proposed changes to the family code have included allowing women to stipulate in their marriage contracts that their husbands cannot take another wife.But exceptions remain, including provisions relating to a first wife's infertility or illness, which women's rights groups have criticised on grounds of privacy and medical confidentiality.These issues are at the heart of proposals to reform the Moudawana, Morocco's family code, which governs marriage, divorce and child custody. A package of changes was announced in 2024, but the reforms have yet to become law.As well as family law, some young women hope the new prime minister will try to improve education for girls.Morocco's High Commission for Planning, the country's official national statistics agency, found in 2025 that just 55% of girls aged 15–17 were going to school in rural areas, where poverty, early marriage and dropping out of school remain key barriers. In urban areas, it was 100%."Many girls in rural Morocco drop out of school early because schools are far away, transport is unsafe or unavailable, and families with limited means often keep their daughters at home," Chifae Laazouzi, a young Moroccan woman, tells the BBC.She says one reason is that many girls in poor and rural areas cannot afford menstrual sanitary products."Menstrual health is still treated as a taboo... I would like to see free menstrual products in schools," Laazouzi says.El Mansouri is no newcomer to politics. Over more than two decades in public life, she has served as mayor of Marrakech, held government posts and sat in parliament.For the past five years, she served as minister for national territory planning, urban planning, housing and city policy under the previous Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch.After her appointment, El Mansouri presented the moment as a milestone for Moroccan women."Being the first female head of government is not just a source of pride for me, but for all the women of the kingdom," she said.Since her appointment, she has not indicated whether she plans to try and push through the reforms to the family code.In her political career so far, she has not made any prominent public statements about women's rights, even while changes to inheritance rules, polygamy and the family code were being widely debated.Dr Irene Fernandez-Molina, an expert on the Global South at the University of Exeter in the UK, sees the appointment in the context of the monarchy's broader political interests."Two headlines have dominated coverage of [September's] parliamentary election in Morocco: a two-decade low turnout and King Mohammed VI's appointment of a woman as prime minister for the first time in this country's history," she tells the BBC."The latter cannot be understood without the former."Official figures put turnout at just 38% of registered voters, while the proportion of all eligible voters who cast a ballot was even lower.Fernandez-Molina describes the appointment as an example of "authoritarian state feminism, a top-down, selective instrumentalisation of the struggle for women's rights for regime legitimation purposes".She argues that promoting a woman to the highest government office might be intended to project an image of modernisation and progress, even when the political system and the pace of social reform remain largely unchanged.For Moroccan women's rights advocate Yasmina Benslimane, the appointment breaks a longstanding barrier, but says El Mansouri's background is also important."It does challenge stereotypes, because it finally breaks a ceiling that was never broken," she says. "But it matters how she got there."El Mansouri's late father was a pasha, a senior local official, and a diplomat. Benslimane argues that her privileged background and access to political networks distinguish her from many Moroccan women who have fewer opportunities to enter public life.For Benslimane, like many women's rights groups in the country, reform of the Moudawana remains a key test of the new government.However, El Mansouri's room for manoeuvre is shaped by the country's political system. The king retains extensive powers over key areas, including defence and foreign affairs, while the head of government operates within a system where authority is shared.When it comes to Moudawana reform, she would have to face the country's religious scholars, who are mostly men.While some Moroccan women welcome her appointment, they say it is what she does as prime minister that really counts."I don't think El Mansouri should be judged by the fact that she is a woman. Being a woman in power doesn't automatically make someone a champion of women's rights," Sara Zouiten, a young Moroccan woman, tells the BBC."Her party presents itself as a modernising political force, so I want to see whether that translates into actual change."You may also be interested in:

schema.headline: Fatima El Mansouri: What can Morocco's first female prime minister change for women?

title: Obama blasts Trump administration probe of congresswoman Ilhan Omar as 'so appalling'
description: Barack Obama has said congresswoman Ilhan Omar is under federal criminal investigation simply because she's an outspoken critic of the President Donal
body: Barack Obama has said congresswoman Ilhan Omar is under federal criminal investigation simply because she's an outspoken critic of the President Donald Trump."The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president," the former US president wrote on X, calling the probe "so appalling".The White House defended the inquiry, saying the justice department was "focused on restoring law and order".Last week, homeland security agents searched the Minnesota Democrat's Washington DC home as part of an investigation into her immigration status. Born in Somalia, Omar moved to the US with her family as a child.US media outlets have reported that the probe is tied to her American citizenship and whether she lied about her age when she arrived in the US in 1995.Questions have been raised about whether the age listed on Omar's citizenship application differed from her actual birth date.Obama said in his X post on Sunday that her father became a naturalised citizen when she was 17, and not yet legally an adult, which then gave her citizenship. "Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen," he wrote."If this becomes the new normal," he added, "there's no reason to believe it will stop with her -  or that future presidents, in either party, won't do the same."According to the US Citizenship and Immigration Services, a child born outside of the US automatically becomes a citizen when he or she has at least one parent who is a citizen by birth or naturalisation, or he or she is under the age of 18, and is a lawful permanent resident living in the custody of a citizen parent. White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis denied the investigation was politically motivated."Unlike Joe Biden, President Trump has not weaponized the Department of Justice against his political foes," she said in an emailed statement to the BBC. "The Department is focused on restoring law and order and keeping Americans safe." Trump has often argued that federal criminal investigations against him as he campaigned for re-election were politically motivated.The investigation into Omar could lead to the justice department seeking to "denaturalise" her, or revoke her citizenship. It would have to prove there were material lies in the naturalisation process.In 2023, Republicans removed Omar from the House Foreign Affairs Committee for comments and tweets she made about Israel, which drew bipartisan criticism.Omar has said that Trump has targeted her for years with "baseless lies and smear campaigns" and called the investigation "the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation". But Trump has said the investigation had "nothing to do" with him, while describing Omar as a "terrible person" and a "complainer".Federal agents reportedly seized her phone, computers, notebooks and passport in the raid a week ago. Her lawyers have demanded the government return her belongings, CBS News, the BBC's US partner, has reported, arguing in a letter sent on Friday that the seizure of property had violated restrictions put in place by a judge to protect her work as a federal lawmaker.The lawyers also alleged agents did not duly notify Omar or the House of Representatives general counsel that a search would be taking place and kept her from contacting her attorney for more than an hour, according to CBS.Democrats characterised the raid as the president attempting to interfere with the legislative branch of government. Republicans, meanwhile, have said Omar should be treated the same as anyone else under the law.When Obama first ran for president, and throughout his two terms in the White House, Trump repeatedly raised questions about his citizenship, asserting he was not born on American soil and was disqualified from serving in office. Obama released two records proving he had been born in Hawaii.Obama did not mention that history in his X post on Sunday.

schema.headline: Obama blasts Trump administration probe of congresswoman Ilhan Omar as 'so appalling'

title: Catalonia's former rebel president can return to Spain, court rules
description: Spain's Supreme Court has ruled the former president of Catalonia, Carles Puigdemont, can return without fear of arrest nearly a decade after going in
body: Spain's Supreme Court has ruled the former president of Catalonia, Carles Puigdemont, can return without fear of arrest nearly a decade after going into self-imposed exile having led a failed independence bid.The court upheld a decision to lift an arrest warrant for him linked to the referendum his regional government organised in 2017, in defiance of Madrid.Direct rule was imposed on the region soon after the vote and Puigdemont fled to Belgium, where he has been based ever since - with a surprise appearance in Barcelona in 2024 prompting a police manhunt.But the Spain to which he may return is much different from a decade ago, with Catalan independence now a marginal political issue.Monday's ruling brings to an end a lengthy legal wrangle between the Spanish judiciary and the former Catalan president.In 2024, Spain's socialist government introduced a controversial amnesty for dozens of Catalan politicians and activists who were involved in the secession drive, but the Supreme Court said Puigdemont and several of his colleagues should be excluded.It argued this was because of the charges against them of alleged financial crimes around staging the referendum.The Constitutional Court overruled that interpretation earlier this month, and on Monday the Supreme Court rejected an appeal by the far-right Vox party against lifting national arrest warrants for Puigdemont, as well as his former ministers Lluís Puig and Toni Comín, paving the way for their return to Spain.Puigdemont was elected as a member of the European Parliament (MEP) in 2019 and to the Catalan parliament in 2024 as leader of the region's centre-right Together for Catalonia (JxCat) party.He had campaigned in the south of France, where he held rallies attended by supporters who travelled across the border to see him.Puigdemont is known to have made at least one brief return to Spain since leaving the country, addressing a crowd of supporters in Barcelona prior to disappearing and escaping back over the border to France before he could be detained.While he was living in Waterloo, Belgium, nine of his former colleagues were jailed for their role in the events of 2017. They were released when the Spanish government pardoned them in 2021.Puigdemont has remained an active political presence, travelling across Europe to espouse the Catalan independence cause and fiercely criticising Spain's democratic institutions.In a video posted on social media just as the Supreme Court ruling was announced, Puigdemont spoke of his reasons for staying abroad."My role was to stir public opinion, internationalise the conflict and work from the heart of Europe to explain the reality of Spain," he said.It is still not known when he might return to Spain.Comín, his former regional minister for health, plans to travel this week to Madrid, where he is due to carry out administrative procedures linked to his status as an MEP.The referendum sparked the country's biggest political crisis since democracy was restored following the death of Francisco Franco.The banned vote was met with a heavy police crackdown. The region's separatist majority declared independence after the vote - Madrid then dissolved parliament, sacked its leaders and called a snap election.But Catalan independence is now a relatively marginal issue in Spain, with housing and immigration dominating the political agenda.The parliamentary support of Puigdemont's JxCat party was instrumental in allowing current Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to form a new left-wing Spanish government after the 2023 election.But within Catalonia, JxCat has been struggling, with a far-right, pro-independence party, Catalan Alliance, taking many of its voters.And next month, Spain's general election could see the far right enter government for the first time.

schema.headline: Catalonia's former rebel president can return to Spain, court rules
